title: Born in India, Remade in Persia
description: Chaturanga, shatranj, a weak counselor, a leaping elephant, and the legends told about where chess came from

concepts.title: Four Limbs of an Army
concepts.contentHtml:
The earliest securely dated Sanskrit mention of chess is a joke about peace. In the Harshacharita, a life of King Harsha of Kannauj written by the court poet Bana around 625 to 640 CE, the poet praises a reign so calm that the only place anyone learned to draw up a chaturanga was on the ashtapada, the board of 8 by 8 squares. The pun works because chaturanga means "having four limbs," the four traditional divisions of an Indian army: elephants, chariots, cavalry and infantry. The joke shows the game was familiar, but Bana says nothing about its rules.

Those divisions survive on every modern board. The chariot became the rook, the horse the knight, the foot soldier the pawn, and the elephant, by a long road, the bishop. Beside the king stood a minister or general who stepped one square diagonally. Because Indian sources are thin, historians reconstruct most of the rules from the later Persian and Arabic game. Some points remain uncertain, and early texts describe the elephant's move in at least three different ways.

The evidence is almost all textual. Gaming pieces from Indus Valley sites have been called proto-chess, but nothing ties them to chaturanga. The mainstream view places the game's birth in northern India by about the 6th century CE. In the 18th and 19th centuries Hiram Cox and Duncan Forbes argued that a four-player dice game, chaturaji, came first; H. J. R. Murray rejected this in 1913, and most scholars agree with him. The translator David H. Li's claim that Chinese chess is the older parent rests, in the historian Peter Banaschak's words, on "virtually nothing."

concepts.title: The King's Riddle from India
concepts.contentHtml:
A Middle Persian text, the Wizarishn i Chatrang ("Explanation of Chess"), tells how an Indian king sent Khosrow I, the Sasanian ruler of Persia (reigned 531 to 579), a chess set of sixteen emerald and sixteen ruby pieces as a test of Persian wisdom. After three days the sage Wuzurgmihr explained the game, then invented nard, an ancestor of backgammon, and sent it back as a counter-riddle. The text reached its final form after the Sasanian era, and scholars treat the story as a legend that follows an old pattern of riddle contests between kings. Ferdowsi's Shahnameh, finished about 1010, retells it.

The legend still records something real: by around 600 CE Persians knew the game as chatrang and thought it came from India. Ivory pieces dug up at Afrasiab near Samarkand, usually dated to around 700 CE though estimates vary, are among the oldest known chessmen. After the Arab conquest of Persia in the 7th century the game became shatranj. The calls "shah!" and "shah mat!" passed into Europe as "check" and "checkmate." Persian mat means roughly "at a loss" or "helpless"; the popular gloss "the king is dead," from the Arabic verb mata, is usually judged a misreading.

Ferdowsi gives a second origin story, also in verse. Two princes, Gav and Talhand, fight over a throne, and Talhand dies on his elephant without a wound, exhausted and surrounded. To show their grieving mother how this could happen, the court sages invent chess, and the poem uses shah mat for Talhand's fate.

concepts.title: A Slow Game of Weak Pieces
concepts.contentHtml:
Shatranj looks like chess but was played very differently. Beside the shah (king) and the rukh (chariot) stood the counselor, the firzan (the European fers), which moved only one square diagonally. The elephant, al-fil, jumped exactly two squares diagonally, leaping whatever stood between; each could reach only 8 of the 64 squares, so the four on the board could never capture one another. Pawns had no double step and promoted only to a firzan. Armies took many moves to meet, and players often aimed for a favored opening setup, a tabiya, largely ignoring the opponent's early moves.

Winning was different too. Checkmate counted, but by most accounts so did stalemating your opponent. Capturing every piece except the king, "baring" it, also won, unless the bare king could take your last piece next move; that was usually a draw, though in Medina it counted as a win. Under the Abbasid caliphs, masters ranked players in classes. Al-Razi beat the leading player al-Adli in 847, and as-Suli, the strongest player of the early 900s, wrote a book on the game. Composers set problems, mansubat, many solved by a chain of checks.

The best-known chess legend grew up in this world. An inventor, often called Sissa, asks his king for one grain of wheat on the first square, two on the second, four on the third, doubling to the 64th. The total, 2 to the power 64 minus 1, is 18,446,744,073,709,551,615 grains, about 1.2 trillion tonnes, more than 1,400 times the world's yearly wheat harvest. The 10th-century writer al-Masudi mentions Indians calculating such a progression, but the inventor's tale is first recorded by Ibn Khallikan in 1256. No historical Sissa is known.

title: The Mad Queen
description: How a Valencian love poem, a printed book and a newly powerful queen turned a slow game into modern chess

concepts.title: A Love Poem in 64 Stanzas
concepts.contentHtml:
Around 1475 in Valencia, three poets turned a game of chess into verse. In Scachs d'amor ("Chess of Love"), written in Valencian, Francesc de Castellví played one side as Mars, Narcís Vinyoles played the other as Venus, and Bernat Fenollar acted as arbiter, commenting on each move and stating the rules. The poem has 64 stanzas of nine lines, one for each square of the board. After three introductory stanzas they come in threes: a move, a reply, and the arbiter's gloss. Love is the allegory, and the players debate it as they go, but the moves form a real game that can be replayed on a board.

The poem is believed to be the earliest documented game played with the modern queen, which moves any distance along a rank, file or diagonal, and the modern bishop, which sweeps the whole length of a diagonal instead of hopping two squares. The opening, 1.e4 d5, is the one now called the Scandinavian Defense, and the game ends in checkmate. Neither player castles or captures en passant, so the poem cannot tell us whether those rules were in use.

The text's survival is itself fragile. The scholar Ignacio Casanovas found the manuscript in 1905 in the library of the Capella del Palau. The original was later lost, and the poem survives through a photograph of the codex kept at the Library of Catalonia in Barcelona. The date of about 1475 is an estimate. Even so, it places the new rules in Valencia some twenty years before they appear in print.

concepts.title: From Counselor to Queen
concepts.contentHtml:
The queen's ancestor was the weak shatranj counselor, the fers. Europeans soon saw a queen in it. A Latin poem preserved at the Swiss monastery of Einsiedeln, usually dated to about 997 and among the earliest European texts on chess, already calls the piece regina, and it is also the first known source for a board of light and dark squares. Around 1300 the fers gained a two-square leap on its first move, but for centuries the queen stayed a short-stepping bodyguard.

In the late 15th century she became the strongest piece on the board, first in Spain. Luis Ramírez de Lucena's Repetición de amores y arte de ajedrez, printed in Salamanca around 1497, is the oldest surviving printed chess book. It analyzes eleven openings and 150 positions, some under the old rules and some under the new. A Valencian chess book by Francesc Vicent, printed in 1495, is lost; the researcher José Antonio Garzón argues that its contents survive in a manuscript found in Cesena, Italy, and that Lucena and Pedro Damiano (Rome, 1512) both drew on it, a case not yet settled. Italians called the new game scacchi alla rabiosa, "madwoman's chess."

Why a queen, and why then? The historian Marilyn Yalom, in Birth of the Chess Queen (2004), suggested that the powerful piece echoed Isabella I of Castile, who ruled in her own right from 1474. She also pointed to the cult of the Virgin Mary and to courtly love. These are suggestions, not proof; no source from the time says the rule honored Isabella. What is clear is the speed of the change. Helped by printing, the new rules spread rapidly through Europe.

concepts.title: Rules That Took Centuries to Settle
concepts.contentHtml:
A faster game rewarded preparation, and opening theory took off. Ruy López de Segura, a Spanish priest, published his Libro de la invención liberal y arte del juego del axedrez at Alcalá de Henares in 1561. He brought the word "gambit," which he had picked up from Italian players, into print, analyzed what became the King's Gambit, and introduced a fifty-move rule, the ancestor of today's. The opening 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 still carries his name.

Other rules wandered for centuries. The pawn's two-square first move appeared sometime between the 13th and 16th centuries and spread slowly. Castling came in many local forms before its modern version settled in France in 1620 and England in 1640, and Italy adopted en passant only in 1880. Stalemate varied most of all. In shatranj it was usually a win for the side that delivered it. Lucena treated it as an inferior victory, worth half the stake in a game played for money. In England, from about 1600 to 1800, the player who stalemated the opponent lost. That English rule disappeared before 1820, replaced by the draw used in France and Italy, though a few English rulebooks went on printing the old version.

Standardization came in the 19th century. In 1849 the London games maker John Jaques released a set designed by Nathaniel Cooke and endorsed by the master Howard Staunton, whose name it still carries; Staunton signed the first 500 sets by hand. Staunton also organized the first international tournament, held in London in 1851 alongside the Great Exhibition. International play pushed national customs toward a single code, and FIDE, the international chess federation, was founded in Paris in 1924.

title: The Mechanical Turk
description: An 18th-century chess automaton, the famous people it met, the legends it gathered, and how its secret came out

concepts.title: A Gift for an Empress
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1770, at Schönbrunn Palace in Vienna, the Habsburg civil servant Wolfgang von Kempelen presented Empress Maria Theresa with a life-size figure in Ottoman robes and a turban, seated behind a wooden cabinet with a chessboard on top. Kempelen, born in Pressburg (now Bratislava) in 1734, had built it after watching a French conjurer, François Pelletier, perform at court in 1769. Audiences called it the Turk. It played chess against all comers, and it usually won.

The show was designed to defeat suspicion. Before a game Kempelen opened the cabinet's doors and drawers to display gears and cylinders inside. Then the Turk moved its pieces with its left arm, nodded when it threatened the queen or gave check, and shook its head at an illegal move. It could also perform the knight's tour, guiding a knight to every square of the board exactly once, a puzzle that many experienced players of the day struggled with.

The machinery was real but beside the point. A strong player sat inside on a sliding seat, shifting as doors opened so that dummy works screened him. Each chess piece had a magnet in its base, which drew up a small magnet on a string beneath that square, so the hidden player could follow the game on the underside of the board. He copied the moves on a small pegboard and worked the Turk's arm through a pantograph linkage, by candlelight, with the smoke carried up through the turban. Kempelen called the invention a trifle and preferred his speaking machine, described in a book in 1791. For about a decade after the debut he often claimed the Turk was under repair to avoid showing it.

concepts.title: Philidor, Franklin and Napoleon
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1783 Kempelen took the Turk on tour: Versailles and Paris, then London, Leipzig and Dresden. In Paris it lost to the Duke of Bouillon and, in a match, to François-André Danican Philidor, the strongest player of his time, who reportedly called it his most fatiguing game ever. Kempelen invited Benjamin Franklin, then the American envoy in France, to see it in May 1783, and that August Franklin praised the "wonderful Machine" in a letter of recommendation. Popular retellings say Franklin played it and lost; that detail rests on later accounts, not on the letters.

After Kempelen died in 1804, his son sold the Turk to the showman and inventor Johann Nepomuk Mälzel. The most famous story dates from 1809, when Napoleon occupied Vienna: he is said to have played the Turk at Schönbrunn, tried illegal moves until it swept the pieces off the board, then lost a real game in 19 moves. The accounts, written decades later, contradict each other; some meeting probably happened, but the details are legend. Napoleon's stepson Eugène de Beauharnais bought the machine in 1811 for 30,000 francs; Mälzel later got it back.

Other stories are plain fiction. A tale that a wounded Polish officer named Worousky hid inside and played Catherine the Great appeared in 1859 under the name of the conjurer Jean-Eugène Robert-Houdin. The historian Tom Standage concludes it "must be dismissed as fiction," though some editions of the Encyclopaedia Britannica repeated it as fact. Claims that Frederick the Great bought the secret have no evidence behind them. On a British tour in 1819 the Turk gave opponents the first move and a pawn, and still won 45 games to 3 losses.

concepts.title: Exposed, Burned and Remembered
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1821 the young engineer Robert Willis argued that a player of ordinary size could hide inside. Mälzel brought the Turk to New York in 1826. In Baltimore in 1827 the heat made its operator, William Schlumberger, faint, and two boys on a nearby rooftop saw him climb out; the Baltimore Gazette reported that the trick had been "discovered by accident," and the public barely noticed. In April 1836 Edgar Allan Poe published "Maelzel's Chess-Player" in the Southern Literary Messenger. He was right that a man was inside, though many of his specific guesses were wrong, and the essay rehearses the reasoning he later gave his detectives.

Schlumberger died of yellow fever in Havana in 1838, and Mälzel died at sea that July on the voyage home. The Turk passed to John Kearsley Mitchell, a Philadelphia physician who had treated Poe. On 5 July 1854 a fire that began in a nearby theater destroyed it in the Philadelphia museum where it stood. Only in 1857 did Mitchell's son, Silas Weir Mitchell, publish the first full explanation, in The Chess Monthly. The chessboard, stored separately, survived, and John Gaughan used it in a working replica he built between 1984 and 1989.

The Turk had imitators. Ajeeb, built by the cabinetmaker Charles Hooper and first shown in London in 1868, was secretly operated at times by the American master Harry Nelson Pillsbury; it burned at Coney Island in 1929. Amazon Mechanical Turk, launched in 2005, borrowed the name for a marketplace where hidden human workers do tasks that software cannot. And Claude Shannon's 1950 paper on chess programming opened its survey of earlier work with Kempelen's automaton and Poe's essay.

title: Chess and the Cold War
description: The Soviet chess machine, Fischer against Spassky in Reykjavik, and the strange title matches that followed

concepts.title: The Soviet Chess Machine
concepts.contentHtml:
In January 1938 Nikolai Krylenko, the Soviet commissar of justice, was denounced at the Supreme Soviet, partly on the charge that "now he devotes a great deal of time to playing chess." He was arrested that month, tried on 29 July in a hearing of about 20 minutes, and shot. Krylenko had done as much as anyone to make chess a Soviet state project. He organized the great Moscow tournament of 1925 and in the 1930s headed the national chess and checkers associations. "We must finish once and for all with the neutrality of chess," he declared, calling for a "Five-Year Plan for chess."

The program was lavish for its time. Moscow 1925, won by Efim Bogoljubov ahead of Emanuel Lasker and José Raúl Capablanca, inspired the comic film Chess Fever by Vsevolod Pudovkin and Nikolai Shpikovsky, in which Capablanca plays himself. Promising players received privileges. After a strong result in 1935, the young electrical engineer Mikhail Botvinnik was given a free car and a 67 percent rise in his study grant; in 1936 he was allowed to take his wife to a tournament in Nottingham; and in wartime Vyacheslav Molotov excused him from war work three days a week to prepare.

The investment paid off. After the champion Alexander Alekhine died in 1946 with the title, FIDE held a match tournament in The Hague and Moscow in 1948, and Botvinnik won it. Soviet players then held the world title without a break until 1972: Botvinnik, Vasily Smyslov, Mikhail Tal, Tigran Petrosian and Boris Spassky. The Soviet team won every Chess Olympiad from 1952 to 1974. Officials presented this as proof of Soviet culture's strength, which made every loss political.

concepts.title: Reykjavik, 1972
concepts.contentHtml:
The title match in Reykjavik began on 11 July 1972 and nearly collapsed within days. The American challenger Bobby Fischer, born in Chicago in 1943, had missed the opening ceremony, forcing a two-day postponement. He lost the first game after playing the capture 29...Bxh2 in a position many expected to be drawn. He then refused to play the second game in the hall because of the television cameras, and the arbiter Lothar Schmid declared it forfeit. Fischer was two points down against the world champion, Boris Spassky.

A phone call from Henry Kissinger, then the US National Security Adviser, had helped persuade Fischer to come at all, and by some accounts to stay after the forfeit. The British financier Jim Slater had already doubled the $125,000 prize fund. For the third game Spassky agreed to play in a small room backstage. Fischer won it, his first win ever against Spassky. When Fischer won the sixth game, Spassky joined the audience in applauding him. The Soviet side later claimed that chemicals or electronic devices were being used to influence Spassky; an Icelandic police sweep was inconclusive.

Spassky resigned the adjourned 21st game on 1 September, and Fischer won 12.5 to 8.5, becoming the first American-born world champion. He never played another official game. In 1975, after FIDE rejected some of his conditions, he refused to defend the title, and Anatoly Karpov became champion by forfeit. His 1992 unofficial rematch with Spassky in Yugoslavia, then under United Nations sanctions, led the United States to issue a warrant for his arrest. Detained in Japan in 2004, he was granted Icelandic citizenship and died in Reykjavik in 2008, aged 64.

concepts.title: Defectors, Yogurt and an Unfinished Match
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1976, after a tournament in Amsterdam, the Soviet grandmaster Viktor Korchnoi asked the English player Tony Miles how to spell "political asylum," then walked into a police station and defected. His wife and son, left behind, were allowed to leave only in 1982. Korchnoi, who settled in Switzerland, still fought his way to a title match against Karpov, held in Baguio in the Philippines from July to October 1978.

Karpov's team included the psychologist and hypnotherapist Vladimir Zukhar, whom Korchnoi accused of trying to hypnotize him from the front rows. Korchnoi's team included two members of the Ananda Marga yoga movement who were out on bail after convictions for attempted murder. Chairs were X-rayed, the flags on the playing table were disputed, and Korchnoi's camp protested that a blueberry yogurt delivered to Karpov during a game might be a coded message. Karpov led 5 to 2, Korchnoi leveled at 5 to 5, and Karpov won the next game to keep the title, 6 to 5 with 21 draws.

Karpov and the young Garry Kasparov began their first match in Moscow on 10 September 1984, with victory going to the first player to win six games. After 48 games and five months, Karpov led 5 to 3 with 40 draws, Kasparov having won the last two. On 15 February 1985 the FIDE president, Florencio Campomanes, stopped the match, citing the players' health. Kasparov said the decision was made to help Karpov. It remains the only world championship match called off without a result. A new 24-game match later in 1985 went to Kasparov, 13 to 11.

title: Machines Learn the Game
description: From a program run with pencil and paper to Shannon's numbers, Deep Blue and a self-taught network

concepts.title: Paper Machines
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1952 Alan Turing played a game of chess on behalf of a computer that could not yet run his program. With David Champernowne he had written, in 1948, rules called Turochamp for choosing moves: look at your moves, the replies and further captures; score the results by material, mobility and king safety; pick the best line by minimax. Turing tried to code it for the Ferranti Mark 1 in 1951 but found it too complex. So against his colleague Alick Glennie he worked through the rules by hand, taking up to about half an hour per move. The program lost in 29 moves.

Others got closer to working hardware. The Spanish engineer Leonardo Torres Quevedo built El Ajedrecista ("The Chess Player"), completed in 1912 and shown in Paris in 1914, an electromechanical machine that played king and rook against a lone king. It read moves through electrical contacts under the board and always delivered checkmate, though not always quickly. In November 1951 a program by Dietrich Prinz for the Ferranti Mark 1 in Manchester solved a mate-in-two problem, usually described as the first chess program to run on a general-purpose computer.

The first win by a computer came on a cut-down board. In 1956 the MANIAC I computer at Los Alamos played chess on a 6 by 6 board with no bishops. It lost to the physicist Martin Kruskal, who played without his queen, but beat a laboratory assistant who had learned the rules the week before: the first computer win over a person at a chess-like game. In 2012 Garry Kasparov played a reconstruction of Turochamp at a Turing centenary conference and won in 16 moves.

concepts.title: Shannon's Arithmetic
concepts.contentHtml:
The founding paper of computer chess came from Claude Shannon, the Bell Labs engineer behind information theory. "Programming a Computer for Playing Chess" appeared in the Philosophical Magazine in March 1950. Shannon chose chess because it was sharply defined, neither trivial nor hopeless, widely thought to require "thinking," and discrete, like a digital computer. Using Adriaan de Groot's data from master games, he put the typical number of legal moves at about 30, so a move and its reply give about 1,000 possibilities, and a game lasts about 40 such pairs. That yields roughly 10 to the power 120 possible games, now called the Shannon number. A machine checking one variation per microsecond, he wrote, would need over 10 to the power 90 years for its first move.

The number is often misquoted. It is a rough count of possible games, not positions, meant only to show that complete calculation was hopeless. Shannon guessed the number of positions at roughly 10 to the power 43; a modern estimate by John Tromp and colleagues puts legal positions at about 4.8 times 10 to the power 44.

Shannon then sketched two designs. A "type A" program examines every move to a fixed depth and scores the results, valuing queen, rook, bishop, knight and pawn at about 9, 5, 3, 3 and 1. A "type B" program searches selectively, following forcing lines further and ignoring pointless ones. In 1968 the international master David Levy bet John McCarthy and other AI researchers a total of £1,250 that no computer would beat him within ten years. He won in 1978, beating Chess 4.7 in a match in Toronto; in 1989 he lost to Deep Thought.

concepts.title: Deep Blue and the Self-Taught Machine
concepts.contentHtml:
On 10 February 1996 in Philadelphia, IBM's Deep Blue beat the world champion Garry Kasparov in a game at a normal tournament time control, the first time a computer had done so. Kasparov still won that match 4 to 2. Deep Blue grew out of ChipTest, begun in 1985 by Feng-hsiung Hsu as a graduate student at Carnegie Mellon University; it became Deep Thought and moved with its team to IBM. The 1997 version, with 480 custom chess chips, could evaluate about 200 million positions a second.

In the New York rematch of May 1997, Deep Blue won 3.5 to 2.5, finishing with a 19-move win in game 6. After losing game 2, Kasparov suggested that human players had intervened. IBM denied it, saying people adjusted the program only between games, declined a rematch, and later published the logs online. A later story holds that a bug produced an odd move in game 1 that unsettled Kasparov; how much it mattered is disputed.

Twenty years later the approach changed. In December 2017 DeepMind described AlphaZero, a program that learned chess from the rules alone by playing against itself, with no opening books or human games. After nine hours of training, it beat the strong open-source program Stockfish 8 in 100 games with 28 wins, 72 draws and no losses, while searching about 80,000 positions per second against Stockfish's 70 million. Critics objected to the conditions, including a fixed minute per move and a small hash table for Stockfish. In the final 2018 paper in Science, with longer time controls and a fairer setup, AlphaZero scored 155 wins and 6 losses in 1,000 games, the rest drawn.

title: Oddities of the Board
description: A brilliant casual game, endgame rules that computers rewrote, and puzzles that make you think backward

concepts.title: The Immortal Game
concepts.contentHtml:
In June 1851, during a break in the first international tournament in London, Adolf Anderssen and Lionel Kieseritzky played a casual game that became more famous than the tournament. Anderssen, a German mathematics teacher, gave up a bishop, then both rooks, then his queen, and mated with his three remaining minor pieces on move 23. Kieseritzky, who lived in Paris, sent the moves to his chess club there, and the magazine La Régence published the game that July. The Austrian master Ernst Falkbeer named it the Immortal Game in 1855.

The game is less clean than its legend. Modern analysts find errors on both sides, and the grandmaster Robert Hübner identifies Black's 11th move as the critical mistake. Kieseritzky himself said he resigned at move 20, before the mating sequence, so the famous final moves may never have been played over the board. Anderssen produced a second showpiece in 1852 against Jean Dufresne, probably in Berlin. In an 1879 tribute after Anderssen's death, Wilhelm Steinitz called one of its moves "an evergreen in the laurel crown of the departed chess hero," and it has been the Evergreen Game ever since.

These games belong to the Romantic era, when players prized attacks, gambits and sacrifices and defense lagged behind. Its best-known short game is the Opera Game of 1858, in which the American Paul Morphy beat Duke Karl II of Brunswick and Count Isouard, consulting together, in 17 moves, in a box at a Paris opera house while the performance went on. Which opera was playing is disputed: one anecdote says Bellini's Norma, other sources Rossini's The Barber of Seville. Anderssen, for his part, won London 1851, a 16-player knockout organized by Howard Staunton.

concepts.title: Rules for the Endgame
concepts.contentHtml:
Chess has a clock built into its rules. Under the fifty-move rule, a player may claim a draw once each side has made fifty moves with no capture and no pawn move. For four centuries after Ruy López set down such a rule, fifty moves seemed generous. Then computers began solving endgames exhaustively, working backward from every checkmate to build tablebases: perfect play for every position with a few pieces. Ken Thompson's tablebase for king and queen against king and rook was used in a 1977 match against the grandmaster Walter Browne.

The computers found wins that took more than fifty moves. FIDE responded with exceptions, allowing first 100 and then 75 moves for a list of endings such as rook and bishop against rook and two knights against a pawn; sources differ on the exact years. In 1992 it abolished the exceptions and restored a strict fifty-move rule for all positions. Since 2014 the arbiter ends the game automatically after 75 moves by each side without a capture or pawn move. The Lomonosov tablebases, completed at Moscow State University in 2012 for all positions with up to seven pieces, kings included, contain a position that is mate in 549 moves.

The same rule caps how long a game can last. Problemists Eero Bonsdorff, Karl Fabel and Olavi Riihimaa calculated in 1966 that a game could run at most 5,899 moves if every draw is claimed as soon as the rule allows; later recalculations give slightly different totals. Real games stop far short. In Belgrade in 1989, Ivan Nikolić and Goran Arsović drew after 269 moves and 20 hours 15 minutes, long the longest tournament game; a decisive game in London in 2024 ran 272 moves.

concepts.title: Puzzles That Run Backward
concepts.contentHtml:
Most chess puzzles ask what happens next. Retrograde analysis asks what happened before. A retro problem shows a position and asks, for example, what the last move was, whether a bishop on its home square must be a promoted pawn, whether a side may still castle, or whether the position could arise at all. A position counts as legal if some sequence of legal moves reaches it, however absurd the game. By convention, castling is assumed allowed unless the position proves the king or rook has moved, while en passant is allowed only if you can prove the previous move was a two-square pawn advance.

The logician Raymond Smullyan popularized the genre with The Chess Mysteries of Sherlock Holmes (1979) and The Chess Mysteries of the Arabian Knights (1981), in which each puzzle is a detective story: the clues are on the board, and the past must be deduced. A related branch, the proof game, asks for the exact moves from the starting position that produce a given position in a stated number of moves.

Backward reasoning also lies behind a theorem about chess. In 1913 the mathematician Ernst Zermelo published a paper applying set theory to chess. Zermelo's theorem says that in a finite game of this kind, either White can force a win, or Black can, or both can force at least a draw. Nobody knows which holds for chess; the game is finite only because of rules on repetition and the fifty-move limit, and the numbers are far too large to search. Checkers, a much smaller game, was solved in 2007 by Jonathan Schaeffer's team at the University of Alberta: perfect play gives a draw.
